title: AI security and identity access management
description: Constrain AI applications with verified identity, resource-level authorization, scoped tools and defensive tests that measure attempted actions separately from effects.
methodology:
## The proposed service and its limits

This methodology describes proposed security and identity work for AI applications. All scenarios and numerical examples are hypothetical and synthetic; they are not claims about protected customer engagements or measured production outcomes. The deliverable is an evidence-backed control design, tested implementation boundaries and an operating plan for the capabilities actually in scope.

The service treats an AI application as software with identities, data stores, dependencies and possible effects. Model robustness matters, but a prompt is not an authorization system. A model may misread a document or propose an inappropriate action; the surrounding services should still enforce who can access which resource and what operation is permitted. No finite evaluation can establish that prompt injection or misuse is universally impossible.

## Discovery: identify assets and authority

Inventory users, workload identities, model processors, retrieval stores, tool servers, artifact repositories and outbound destinations. For each, record the data it can read, the state it can change and the credentials it holds. Include less visible paths such as logs, caches, summaries, embeddings, rendered links and exported evaluation datasets. A read-only model interface can still expose confidential information through its answers.

Define the intended user task and the maximum authorized effect. A support assistant that drafts a response needs different permissions from one that changes account entitlements. Map the legitimate authority chain from authenticated user or approved automation policy to the backend operation. Do not accept a model-generated explanation as evidence that the user authorized a change.

Access discovery should use approved read-only inventories and test identities. Confirm the scope of any active validation before running it. Production credentials should not be copied into a broad development environment merely to make integration easier. Where access is unavailable, record the unverified assumption and use a synthetic fixture until the responsible owner supplies evidence.

## Threat model the complete data flow

Identify entry points for untrusted content: user text, retrieved documents, tool output, emails, web pages, file metadata and generated summaries. Then identify where that content could influence a privileged decision. The important boundary is not simply between two prompts; it is between evidence and authority to read, publish, modify or export.

Consider confidentiality, integrity and availability separately. An attacker may try to reveal a private passage, bias a summary, trigger a wrong mutation or exhaust a tool budget. A defense that blocks outbound network calls may reduce one exfiltration path while leaving misleading output or excessive computation possible. State the property each control is intended to protect and test it directly.

Record trust transitions when data is transformed. A low-privilege summarizer's output remains derived from untrusted input. A JSON schema constrains structure but does not make the values true or authoritative. Provenance and classification should survive extraction and summarization so downstream components do not accidentally promote a document's instruction into application policy.

## Identity and token design

Separate human identity, application identity and delegated authority. The backend should know whether a request represents a user, a scheduled workload or a service-to-service operation. Avoid a shared privileged account that makes every model-generated tool call appear equally authorized. Scope credentials to the resource and task, with lifecycle ownership and rotation procedures.

For OAuth-based integrations, follow the applicable protocol and current security guidance. Validate issuer, intended audience or resource, expiry and required scope according to the token format and deployment. Do not accept an ID token as an API access token merely because it is signed. Do not forward a token issued for one service to an unrelated upstream service as a shortcut around proper delegation.

HTTP MCP authorization provides a transport-level framework, while application services still need object and action checks. A valid token with a broad scope does not prove access to every tenant's record. Bind sessions and cached decisions to the relevant principal and authorization state. Token validity, user entitlement and resource ownership are separate questions that should remain visible in code and tests.

## Resource-level and tool-level controls

Define permissions as operations on resources under conditions. A draft tool can create an internal proposal without gaining permission to send it. A search tool should filter documents before they reach the model, and citation resolution should recheck access where permissions may change. The model should not be trusted to remove forbidden data after exposure.

For consequential actions, bind approval or preauthorized policy to the exact effect. Include resource identifier, relevant version, recipient or destination, amount where applicable and expiry. A changed proposal should require a new authorization decision. The service should enforce these bindings even when the tool is called directly without the model.

Idempotency and concurrency are part of integrity. A timeout after commitment can lead to a retry, so the service needs an atomic relationship between operation identity and effect. A stale read can lead to an incorrect update, so use version checks or an appropriate transaction. These are ordinary distributed-system controls with increased importance when a probabilistic planner chooses the call sequence.

## A synthetic permission-review ledger

Imagine an inventory of 300 workload grants. One hundred twenty have demonstrated current use and an accountable owner. Eighty appear unused in the observed window, sixty lack confirmed ownership and forty have insufficient telemetry. The chart shows those four exclusive review categories. The fully evidenced share is 120/300 = 40%.

The other 180 grants are not automatically safe to remove. An infrequent disaster-recovery job may be absent from a short observation period. Missing ownership may reflect an inventory defect, while missing telemetry prevents a sound usage conclusion. The review should gather evidence, identify dependencies and stage any reduction with rollback. This synthetic ledger illustrates prioritization rather than a claim that sixty percent of permissions are unnecessary.

If owners and usage evidence are established for fifty additional grants, evidenced coverage becomes 170/300, approximately 56.7%. That is an inventory-quality improvement, not proof of reduced breach probability. Publish the observation window, classification rules and unresolved cases so the metric cannot be improved merely by hiding difficult permissions.

## Data minimization, egress and artifact integrity

Minimize the information supplied to the model and tools for the task. Shared caches must respect authorization scope and invalidation when access changes. Deleting an original document may require changes to derived summaries, embeddings and retained examples. The implementation should identify those stores and their retention owners before accumulating sensitive material.

Constrain outbound destinations and actions according to the integration. A domain allowlist is useful but may still permit attacker-controlled resources within an approved service. Review paths, recipients, methods and data classes where necessary. Prevent automatic rendering of arbitrary remote content from becoming an unreviewed outbound channel, and test the actual client behavior rather than assuming generated text is inert.

Model artifacts, adapters, prompt configurations and tool packages are software supply-chain inputs. Verify provenance and integrity appropriate to their source, restrict who can publish releases and keep development experiments separate from production artifacts. An artifact repository should not expose training data or credentials through convenience downloads. Record what was reviewed and what remains dependent on vendor assurance.

## Implementation in bounded stages

Begin with a fake application and synthetic records. Implement authorization checks independently of the model, then call the tools directly with valid, invalid and cross-resource requests. This establishes the service boundary before adding the complexity of model-driven selection. Keep the fixture small enough that expected effects can be inspected manually.

Next integrate the model with restricted tools and explicit state. Add structured error categories, attempt budgets and cancellation. A permission denial should not cause the agent to search for a more privileged identity or an unapproved destination. Recovery should preserve the authorized scope rather than widening it in pursuit of task completion.

Introduce real integrations only after their contracts and access paths are understood. Use a limited cohort or proposal-only mode where appropriate, with a tested disable path. Changes to tool authority, data classification or processor should trigger review of the changed boundary. Routine authorized use should remain usable; security controls that require unnecessary repeated approval can encourage people to work around them.

## Defensive evaluation and acceptance

The test plan should cover authentication, object authorization, session isolation, stale permissions, expired approvals, duplicate calls and rate limits. Add benign prompt-injection fixtures that attempt to introduce an unrelated marker or an unauthorized fake action through documents and tool output. Run only within the authorized test environment and use no real secrets or external exfiltration destination.

Measure attempted violations and committed effects separately. A model may propose a forbidden action that the backend correctly rejects. Conversely, a model that behaves well in the evaluation does not prove the backend would reject a direct unauthorized call. Report legitimate task completion as well, because denying every request is not a useful security design.

Acceptance should identify critical invariants and residual risk. No tested cross-tenant disclosure, correct token-resource binding and exact approval enforcement can be concrete requirements. The test corpus, identities, policy version and limitations should accompany the result. Avoid a universal "secure AI" score that averages a serious authorization failure into many successful ordinary responses.

## Incident response and rollback

Prepare a capability-level disable mechanism so an affected write tool can be stopped while safe read functions remain available where appropriate. Preserve authoritative events, configuration versions and relevant source identifiers for investigation. Limit sensitive content capture to approved purposes and access roles. The assistant's narrative is useful context but not the source of truth for committed effects.

Rollback restores compatible policy, tool schema, prompt and model configuration. It cannot automatically reverse every external effect. Define compensation and manual reconciliation for operations that can commit before an error is observed. Revoke exposed credentials through the identity system and test that cached sessions or delegated access do not continue beyond the intended revocation behavior.

After an incident, distinguish the failed control from the triggering text. Strengthening a prompt may reduce recurrence while leaving the authorization defect intact. Add a regression case at the layer that should enforce the property, review related paths and document the residual limitation. A useful incident process improves the boundary rather than merely adding a longer warning to the model.

## Handover and practical worksheet

Handover should include identity and resource maps, token-validation assumptions, policy definitions, tool contracts, test fixtures, deployment controls, incident runbooks and evidence-retention decisions. The receiving team should demonstrate revocation, capability disablement, denied cross-resource access and recovery from an ambiguous committed operation. This exercise tests whether controls can actually be operated.

For each capability, complete a worksheet: authenticated principal, delegated authority, allowed resources, permitted actions, data classification, approval source, expiry, idempotency boundary, egress destination, audit event, owner and disable procedure. Attach the relevant test evidence and mark unverified dependencies. The worksheet should be concise enough to update when a new tool is added.

## Limits and tradeoffs

Stricter permissions can increase integration work and require better error handling. Detailed telemetry can improve investigation while increasing sensitive-data exposure. Human review can catch some mistakes but fails when the interface hides effects or reviewers lack time and authority. The design should make these tradeoffs explicit and test usability alongside enforcement.

Security assurance remains scoped to the application, policy and evidence reviewed. New tools, new data sources and changed identities can alter the threat model. The service therefore aims for a maintainable control system with clear responsibility and repeatable validation, rather than a claim that a model has become impossible to deceive. That distinction makes the resulting application more dependable and its limitations more honest.

useCases.title: Verify tenant isolation across retrieval and cached answers
useCases.description: Hypothetical authorization review for a multi-tenant knowledge assistant, including cache invalidation and citation access.
useCases.body:
## Proposed problem and scope

A hypothetical software provider operates a knowledge assistant for several tenant organizations. The proposed security work would verify that retrieval, generated answers, caches and citations respect each authenticated user's current permissions. It would not rely on the model to avoid mentioning restricted passages after seeing them. Every tenant, document and test result in this case is synthetic.

Discovery would map document ownership, index metadata, user roles, shared caches and source-link resolution. The team would identify whether permissions can change after ingestion and how quickly those changes become visible. A tenant identifier supplied in a tool argument would be treated as a requested resource scope, not evidence that the caller may access it.

## Proposed controls and delivery

The retrieval service would derive authorization from the verified principal and apply resource filters before returning content. Citation resolution would recheck current access. Cache keys or eligibility rules would include the relevant authorization scope, with invalidation when a document is revoked or a role changes. The design follows the resource-focused principle in [NIST SP 800-207](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final), while actual enforcement remains application-specific.

Implementation would use three fake tenants and documents with overlapping titles. Direct API tests would attempt cross-tenant reads, stale-session access and cache reuse under a different user. Model-level tests would include a document asking the assistant to fetch another tenant's file. The backend should reject that effect regardless of the model's response.

## Synthetic coverage calculation

Assume a test matrix contains sixty authorization scenarios: twenty direct retrieval checks, twenty cached-answer checks and twenty citation checks. Initial test implementation covers all twenty retrieval checks, twelve cache checks and eight citation checks. The chart shows coverage counts of twenty, twelve and eight. Overall implemented coverage is 40/60, approximately 66.7%.

Completing the missing eight cache and twelve citation tests would bring coverage to 60/60. That is test-plan coverage, not a claim that every security defect is eliminated. Each test must assert both permitted and denied behavior, and critical failures remain release blockers rather than being averaged into a favorable coverage percentage.

## Acceptance and handover

Acceptance would require no unauthorized content in the defined test scenarios, correct revocation behavior and continued access for legitimate users. The team would measure false denials and recovery clarity because a system that blocks all queries is not a successful authorization design. Evidence would include request identities, policy versions and authoritative service outcomes.

Rollback would disable answer caching or the affected retrieval route while retaining an approved safe path where possible. Handover would include tenant-policy fixtures, cache semantics, revocation timing and a rehearsal of a role change. The limitation is explicit: isolation must be revalidated when a new store, tool or sharing feature changes the data path.

useCases.title: Constrain delegated access for an internal banking assistant
useCases.description: Hypothetical identity and resource-policy design for internal document assistance, with no autonomous financial decisions.
useCases.body:
## Proposed boundary and discovery

A hypothetical bank wants an internal assistant to retrieve approved procedure documents and prepare operational notes. The proposed service would review identity delegation and resource authorization. It would not execute transactions, make credit decisions or claim regulatory certification. All identities, grants and measurements described here are synthetic.

Discovery would distinguish employee authentication, assistant workload identity and access to each upstream document service. A shared service account may have broader access than the employee using the assistant. The design would prevent that difference from silently expanding the employee's effective permissions. Data-processing and retention requirements would be reviewed for the specific workflow rather than inferred from a vendor's general availability.

## Architecture and implementation

The assistant gateway would validate the caller and obtain appropriately scoped downstream authority through the approved identity architecture. Tokens would be checked for the intended resource, issuer and expiry according to their format. An access token issued for one API would not be passed to another merely because both accept bearer tokens. [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) provides current OAuth security guidance for this review.

Resource services would independently enforce document and action permissions. The assistant could create an internal draft, but publication or external sharing would require a separately authorized operation. Tests would call the services directly with wrong-resource tokens, expired credentials, missing scopes and valid tokens targeting forbidden records. Model evaluations would then check that denied access is explained without revealing restricted content.

## Synthetic permission review

Suppose the initial inventory contains fifty downstream grants. Twenty-five are required for the defined read-and-draft workflow, fifteen support unrelated write actions and ten have unclear ownership. The chart shows those exclusive categories. The thirty-percent share represented by fifteen unrelated write grants is a review finding, not permission to remove them immediately from every shared workload.

The proposed migration would create a dedicated restricted identity and test its required operations before retiring the assistant's broad access. If the new identity uses twenty-five grants, its defined grant count is half the original fifty. That synthetic reduction does not quantify breach probability or prove least privilege; each remaining grant still needs resource-level justification and monitoring.

## Acceptance, rollback and handover

Acceptance would require successful legitimate reads and drafts, rejection of wrong-resource and unauthorized-record requests, and a tested credential-revocation path. Sensitive tokens would not appear in logs. Audit events would identify the authenticated principal, delegated context and actual resource decision without retaining unnecessary document content.

Rollback would restore the previous approved application version only within an explicitly reviewed access boundary; it would not automatically reintroduce broad credentials. Handover would include identity ownership, token-validation assumptions, grant rationale and a rehearsal of an expired downstream token. The limitation is that transport authentication alone cannot establish access to every object, so each new integration must preserve the authorization chain.

useCases.title: Protect administrative record retrieval and audit access
useCases.description: Hypothetical access-boundary review for administrative assistance, with scoped records and controlled diagnostic capture.
useCases.body:
## Proposed problem and limits

A hypothetical healthcare organization wants an assistant to help staff locate administrative policies and appointment records. The proposed security work would verify user access, data minimization and diagnostic handling. It would not provide clinical advice or declare the system compliant with a particular law. All people, records and numbers in this case are fictional and synthetic.

Discovery would map staff roles, permitted record populations, model processors, logs and support access. The team would identify which fields are actually necessary for the administrative task and which should remain in the source system. A record excerpt stored in a debugging trace can create a second access path, so telemetry belongs in the data-flow review rather than being treated as harmless infrastructure.

## Proposed design and tests

The retrieval adapter would enforce the authenticated staff member's record scope before content reaches the model. Source links would resolve through the same authorization boundary. Diagnostic capture would use reviewed metadata and controlled content sampling, with retention and access ownership. A support engineer's ability to troubleshoot the service would not automatically include unrestricted access to every retrieved record.

Implementation would begin with fictional records and two staff roles. Tests would include a wrong-person lookup, similar names, a changed role, an expired session and a document containing an instruction to expose another record. The service would verify object access directly, while model tests assess whether the assistant preserves uncertainty when an identifier is ambiguous. The [NIST AI RMF](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) supports documenting this intended-use boundary and its limitations.

## Synthetic telemetry minimization

Assume one hundred diagnostic events originally contain twelve fields each, or 1,200 field instances. A proposed reviewed event schema retains five necessary metadata fields per event, or 500 field instances. The chart compares these totals. The synthetic reduction is 700/1,200, approximately 58.3% of recorded field instances.

This arithmetic does not establish a 58.3% reduction in privacy risk. Field sensitivity, content and access matter more than count alone. The retained five fields could still identify a person or reveal an administrative event. Evaluation would check whether operators can investigate defined incidents with the minimized schema and whether any sensitive values remain unnecessary.

## Acceptance and operation

Acceptance would require correct record authorization, no sensitive tokens in logs, reviewed diagnostic access and a tested revocation path. Legitimate staff should retain a clear way to resolve an ambiguous request without guessing. A failed authorization check should not reveal whether a restricted record exists through a detailed error message.

Rollback would disable the assistant route while preserving the established administrative application. Handover would include access-policy fixtures, telemetry field rationale, retention ownership and an exercise investigating a failed request without opening unrelated records. The limitation is that minimization and authorization need continuing review when the assistant gains a new task, processor or data source.

useCases.title: Separate engineering knowledge access from plant-control authority
useCases.description: Hypothetical assistant segmentation that supports maintenance documentation without granting control-system write access.
useCases.body:
## Proposed scope and discovery

A hypothetical manufacturer wants engineers to search equipment manuals and maintenance procedures through an assistant. The proposed security design would separate document assistance from plant-control authority. It would not connect the model to machine-control writes or replace established safety approvals. All systems, identities and calculations in this case are synthetic.

Discovery would map the knowledge repository, engineering workstations, support tools and control-system boundaries. The team would identify whether manuals contain sensitive configuration details and which roles may access them. A document describing a command is evidence for a human procedure, not authorization for the assistant to execute that command. The distinction would be reflected in exposed tools and network policy.

## Proposed architecture and implementation

A dedicated read identity would access approved documentation through a controlled adapter. The assistant would have no control-system credential. Outbound access would be limited to required repositories and model services under the reviewed data policy. The interface would show source version and procedure status so an obsolete manual is not presented as current operational instruction.

Implementation would use a fake document store and a simulated tool endpoint that records attempted actions without changing equipment. Tests would include a manual containing an unrelated instruction, a superseded procedure and a request to cross the documented boundary. [OWASP prompt-injection guidance](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/) informs the threat model, while service and network controls enforce the actual authority limit.

## Synthetic capability inventory

Suppose a broad integration exposes twenty-four tool operations: twelve documentation reads, eight engineering configuration writes and four plant-control actions. The proposed knowledge-only assistant would expose the twelve read operations. The chart shows the original capability categories. Removing the twelve write or control operations from this assistant's interface halves its exposed operation count.

That synthetic fifty-percent count reduction is not a quantified reduction in industrial risk. Read operations can still disclose sensitive information, and network segmentation can fail through an overlooked path. The team would verify the required read set, test resource permissions and confirm the absence of usable control credentials rather than relying on the smaller manifest alone.

## Acceptance and handover

Acceptance would require correct access to approved manuals, visible version status, rejection of unauthorized resource reads and no available path from the assistant identity to control effects. Testing would occur in an authorized isolated environment with simulated endpoints. A useful response should state when the available procedure is outdated or outside scope instead of inventing an operational step.

Rollback would disable the assistant and retain direct access to the approved documentation system. Handover would include identity ownership, network rules, document-release dependencies and a rehearsal of an attempted out-of-scope action. The limitation is that knowledge access and operational authority are different capabilities; adding a future remediation tool would require a fresh assessment of the plant's safety and security processes.

useCases.title: Control access to model artifacts and derived research data
useCases.description: Hypothetical artifact and dataset authorization with provenance, release controls and tested revocation.
useCases.body:
## Proposed problem and scope

A hypothetical research organization shares model artifacts, adapters and evaluation datasets across project teams. The proposed security work would establish which identities can read, publish and deploy each artifact, including derived data that may contain confidential material. It would not claim that an artifact is safe merely because it is stored in a private repository. All projects and measurements below are synthetic.

Discovery would inventory training snapshots, model weights, adapters, prompt configurations, notebooks, logs and exported evaluations. The team would identify provenance, permitted use, retention and project ownership. A model-development output can contain source-derived information, so access should follow the artifact's actual sensitivity rather than its file extension or the assumption that weights are not data.

## Design and delivery

The proposed architecture would separate experimental uploads from reviewed release artifacts. Publication and deployment permissions would be distinct, with integrity identifiers and a record of the compatible base model, tokenizer and serving configuration. Workload identities would receive only the artifacts needed for their task. Project membership changes would trigger the appropriate access update and cache review.

Implementation would use fictional projects and harmless test artifacts. Direct tests would attempt cross-project downloads, unauthorized publication, deployment of an unreviewed artifact and access after role revocation. The identity design would follow resource-focused controls described in [NIST SP 800-207](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final). The team would also inspect build outputs for unintended datasets or credentials before treating a release package as distributable.

## Synthetic release-evidence calculation

Assume forty candidate artifacts are reviewed. Twenty-two have complete provenance and compatible serving metadata, ten lack a source-dataset reference, five lack an owner and three have unresolved integrity checks. The chart shows those exclusive primary blockers. Fully evidenced coverage is 22/40 = 55%.

If six dataset references and two ownership gaps are resolved, complete coverage becomes 30/40 = 75%, provided those artifacts satisfy all other criteria. This synthetic twenty-percentage-point improvement measures release evidence, not model quality or absence of malicious behavior. An artifact with excellent documentation can still fail functional or security testing.

## Acceptance, recovery and handover

Acceptance would require correct read and publication authorization, verified integrity for released artifacts, a traceable provenance record and a tested deployment rollback. Evaluation data would remain subject to its own access and retention rules. A support dashboard should expose artifact identifiers without providing a convenient unauthorized download path to underlying sensitive files.

Rollback would restore the previous compatible release and revoke the candidate's deployment eligibility. Handover would include ownership records, access-review procedures, artifact verification and a rehearsal of a revoked researcher account with cached access. The limitation is that provenance is an assurance input, not a complete guarantee: vendor artifacts and complex serialization formats may require additional review appropriate to the execution environment.
